newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian military pledges neutrality but threats remain.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian military pledges neutrality but threats remain.

text.p: Cambodia's armed forces eased coup fears last week by pledging political neutrality, but analysts said they would take sides if the units guarding the country's two rival premiers began fighting each other.

"The (140,000-member) armed forces, I think, will remain neutral...generally they are staying put in their barracks," said a Western military analyst. "What our concern would be is if something were started between the bodyguards in town, how would you then stop that spreading to a larger situation."
"Once the firing starts all bets are off... I'm talking about real clashes," the analyst said, adding that the eruption of fierce fighting "would have a snowballing effect".
Co-Interior Minister Sar Kheng on Friday said defence and security officials from both parties in the feuding coalition government had pledged to avoid bloodshed and remain neutral.

The promise followed several days of rumours that an escalating row between co-premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh of the royalist FUNCIPEC party and Hun Sen of the rival Cambodian People's Party (CPP) would soon culminate in a coup.

The two men formed an uneasy coalition government after U.N.-run elections in 1993. Their relationship has steadily deteriorated since a deadly March 30 grenade attack on a political rally led by opposition leader and FUNCINPEC ally Sam Rainsy, who has blamed Hun Sen for the attack.
Relations worsened further this month when Hun Sen said the CPP supported royalist dissidents who had challenged Ranariddh's leadership of FUNCINPEC.

The Western military analyst said he believed the armed forces chief of staff, General Ke Kim Yan of the CPP, genuinely wished to remain neutral. But he noted that the general did not control the substantial forces protecting the two premiers.
Military experts estimate Ranariddh and Hun Sen can each count on the protection of a battalion of soldiers backed by tanks and artillery and based in the suburbs of Phnom Penh.
Hun Sen spends much of his time at a country residence dubbed the "Tiger's Lair" and protected by armed forces. Both premiers travel with large military escorts.

"I hope the two parties are wise enough not to ask for military backup," CPP legislator Khieu Kanharith said last week. "If the army does not get involved, it's okay. I think we can settle it (the political feud) peacefully."

Analysts said signs of polarisation in the army had emerged after the order to halt an advance on the last big base of hardline Khmer Rouge guerrillas in the country's northwest due to the political crisis in Phnom Penh.

"Before, the armed forces seemed to be neutral, but when the crisis in Phnom Penh erupted the troops started separating and listening to their own commanders, so both sides are building up their muscle," one army general in the northwest said last week.
Lao Mong Hay, director of the Khmer Institute of Democracy, said it was not in the interests of top commanders to start fighting but that others in the military might act irrationally.

"I discount the prospect of the military staging any coup or having prolonged clashes because it's not in the interest of military commanders," he said, noting that they risked losing comfortable positions and good sources of income.

Analysts believe the pledge of neutrality may temporarily reduce tensions but that friction between the premiers will resurface and the military's neutrality again be tested ahead of 1998 elections. "We might be over the hump and working our way back into the next trough," said the military analyst.
